title: The Home Front and Incarceration
objective: After this level you can explain how World War II changed work for women and Black Americans, and why Japanese Americans were forced into camps.
summary: World War II put six million women into war jobs and pushed Black Americans to demand a double victory, while Executive Order 9066 forced about 122,000 Japanese Americans into camps.

cards.headline: In 1942 the government forced about 122,000 Japanese Americans from their homes.
cards.body: The same war opened factory gates to women and Black workers. How could one war widen freedom for some and take it from others?

cards.headline: Rosie and the Double V
cards.body: More than six million women took wartime factory jobs; Rosie the Riveter became their symbol. Labor leader A. Philip Randolph threatened to bring tens of thousands of Black marchers to Washington unless defense jobs opened to them. The result was Executive Order 8802 of June 25, 1941: "There shall be no discrimination in the employment of workers in defense industries." In 1942 the Pittsburgh Courier launched the Double V campaign: victory over fascism abroad and racism at home.

cards.headline: Executive Order 9066
cards.body: Executive Order 9066, issued February 19, 1942, led to the forced removal of about 122,000 Japanese Americans from the West Coast. Nearly 70,000 of them were US citizens. None were charged with a crime, and they had no way to appeal. The government called the guarded camps "relocation centers"; they were also known as "internment camps." This level uses the plainer word: incarceration.

cards.headline: Fighting back, and an apology
cards.body: Gordon Hirabayashi and Fred Korematsu challenged the orders in court, but the Supreme Court upheld them. More than 30,000 Japanese Americans served in the war, in segregated units. In 1988 Congress apologized for the incarceration and paid $20,000 to each person who had been held.

cards.headline: The Home Front and Incarceration: explained

Randolph's threatened march won Executive Order 8802
About 122,000 Japanese Americans were incarcerated without charges
